Hi, yeah, thanks. So, I'm mostly here because I’ve started planning my whole day around, well, not using elevators. It’s getting a bit out of hand. But the real issue is how it's messing with my job. I've never been to Arizona, but I hear the heat is a dry heat, so maybe it's not too bad compared to here? But anyway, Arthur's building doesn’t really have another option besides the elevator, like the stairs are locked or something, so I just had to stop seeing him. I just can't do the elevator thing, and it's starting to get in the way.

I think it's just elevators specifically. Like, I know an elevator in a nice, modern office block is probably completely safe, right? But when I look at those old, clunky doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at my work, my mind just immediately goes to this place where I'm convinced I'm about to get trapped in there, or the cables are going to snap and drop me. Even though part of me knows that sounds totally over the top and dramatic. 

Actually, the elevator at my work is the absolute worst. I work as a training specialist for this corporate tech company, and our building is from, like, the 1970s. The carpet in the hallways is this hideous orange and brown geometric pattern. It honestly looks like something out of a bad sci-fi movie. I was actually talking to the facilities manager about it last week—nice guy, his name is Dave, always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts. He was telling me that they're finally going to renovate the whole floor next spring. They're going to put in hardwood, or well, that fake laminate stuff that looks like hardwood, which is probably easier to clean anyway. I spilled coffee on that orange carpet on my second day of work, and let me tell you, getting a stain out of 40-year-old carpet is impossible. I tried club soda, dish soap, everything. I ended up just having to put a potted plant over the spot so my boss wouldn't see it. It's a snake plant, actually, because I read they're impossible to kill, and I have a terrible track record with plants.

I don't know, maybe? If I had like a joystick or something and I could steer it? But elevators don't really work like that, do they? You just push a button and hope for the best. It's not like driving a forklift.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I mean, I don't really know if having someone with me would make a difference. Maybe? But honestly, I usually just take the stairs anyway, even when I'm with other people. 

Like, the other day I was getting lunch with my coworker, Sarah. We were going to this new deli that opened up down the street from our office. They have these amazing pastrami sandwiches—like, the meat is stacked so high you can barely get your mouth around it. And they make their own pickles in-house, which are super crunchy and garlicky. Anyway, Sarah is one of those people who always wears heels, even though our office is pretty casual. She has this massive collection of them under her desk. She was complaining about her feet hurting and wanted to take the elevator down from the fourth floor, and I just told her I'd meet her in the lobby. I just took the stairs. 

I've gotten pretty fast at taking the stairs, actually. I try to skip every other step on the way down, it kind of feels like a workout. I used to run cross-country in high school, so I guess I still have some of that stamina. We had this coach, Coach Miller, who would make us run hills in the pouring rain. He used to say it built character, but I think he just liked watching us suffer. 

But yeah, I don't know if having someone with me in the elevator would help. I haven't really tried it lately because I just avoid them altogether.

I don't really know if that would help, honestly. Knowing someone is watching... I mean, who is watching? Is it just some guy in a basement somewhere? 

Because my buddy Greg used to work security for this big office building downtown, and his whole job was basically just watching camera feeds. He said it was the most boring job in the world. Control the doors? Like... having a button that actually works to hold them open or force them open? I mean, maybe that would give me a little peace of mind right before getting in, but once they close, you're still trapped in the box, right?

I went to his apartment to pick it up, and he had literally, I kid you not, like five massive parrots just flying free in his living room. We ended up at this overlook that was crazy high up, just a sheer drop-off. And I felt totally fine standing near the edge. \n\nWe actually brought a picnic up there. Sandwiches from this little deli near my place. They make this incredible spicy Italian sub, like, they use this special pepper relish that just makes the whole thing. I've tried to recreate it at home, but I can never get the vinegar ratio right. I think they might use some sort of artisan balsamic or something. But yeah, standing up there, looking out over the whole valley while eating that sandwich... it was great. No panic at all. So, no, it's definitely not a height thing.\n\nDoctor: What exactly do you think might happen if you were to get trapped in an elevator?\n\nPatient: I don't know, honestly. I guess I just picture the doors getting stuck and me just... being stuck in there forever. Or until the air runs out. Which I know doesn't actually happen, they aren't airtight. I saw this documentary once about how buildings are ventilated, and it's actually super fascinating. They have all these massive ducts and fans up on the roof, and the system is designed to keep the air pressure balanced throughout the whole building. \n\nThe guy in the documentary was explaining how they have to clean those ducts, and it looked like the worst job ever. They send these little remote-controlled robots with cameras and brushes on them down into the vents. I actually looked up how much those robots cost because I thought it would be a cool toy to mess around with, maybe attach a camera to it and see what my cat does when it chases him around the apartment. My cat, Barnaby, he's a trip. He's this orange tabby, and he has this weird obsession with knocking my pens off the desk. Every single time I sit down to work, swat, swat, there goes the pen. I had to buy a special heavy-duty pen holder just to keep him out of it. \n\nBut, um... yeah, getting trapped. I just... I don't really know what would happen, but the thought of it just makes my chest tight.\n\nDoctor: Is it the thought of being in a small, enclosed space like an elevator that scares you, or is it something more specific about elevators themselves?\n\nPatient: I think it's just elevators specifically. Like, I know an elevator in a nice, modern office block is probably completely safe, right? But when I look at those old, clunky doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at my work, my mind just immediately goes to this place where I'm convinced I'm about to get trapped in there, or the cables are going to snap and drop me. Even though part of me knows that sounds totally over the top and dramatic. \n\nActually, the elevator at my work is the absolute worst. I work as a training specialist for this corporate tech company, and our building is from, like, the 1970s. The carpet in the hallways is this hideous orange and brown geometric pattern. It honestly looks like something out of a bad sci-fi movie. I was actually talking to the facilities manager about it last week—nice guy, his name is Dave, always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts. He was telling me that they're finally going to renovate the whole floor next spring. They're going to put in hardwood, or well, that fake laminate stuff that looks like hardwood, which is probably easier to clean anyway. I spilled coffee on that orange carpet on my second day of work, and let me tell you, getting a stain out of 40-year-old carpet is impossible. I tried club soda, dish soap, everything. I ended up just having to put a potted plant over the spot so my boss wouldn't see it. It's a snake plant, actually, because I read they're impossible to kill, and I have a terrible track record with plants. \n\nBut yeah... what was I saying? Oh, right. The old doors. Yeah, looking at those old elevator doors just makes my brain think I'm going to get stuck or dropped, even if I know it's probably fine.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is because you feel like you're not in control when you're inside one?\n\nPatient: I mean, maybe? I haven't really thought about it like that. Control is a weird thing, you know? Like, I guess I don't have control in an elevator, but I also don't have control when I'm flying, or even just sitting in the passenger seat of a car. \n\nMy buddy Mike, the one with the Jeep I mentioned earlier, he is the absolute worst driver. We were driving down to the city last weekend to go to this vintage arcade bar—they have all these classic pinball machines, which are so hard to find in good working condition nowadays. I spent like twenty bucks just playing the Addams Family pinball machine. The flippers on it were perfectly calibrated, it was awesome. But anyway, Mike was driving us down there, and we got stuck in this massive traffic jam on the interstate. Just bumper to bumper for miles because of some construction. I had zero control over the situation, just sitting there in the passenger seat listening to him complain about the brake lights in front of us. \n\nHe was listening to this podcast about deep-sea diving, which honestly sounded terrifying. Just annoyed that we were going to be late for the arcade. So... yeah, I don't really know if it's a control thing with the elevators. Dog food, cat litter, those giant scratching posts... you wouldn't believe how heavy a pallet of clumping cat litter is. I had to take this two-day training course, and the instructor was this old guy named Earl who chewed on unlit cigars the entire time. Never lit them, just chewed on them. He was super strict about the speed limit in the warehouse, which was like five miles an hour. It felt like you were crawling. But honestly, driving that forklift was kind of fun once I got the hang of it. You use these levers to tilt the forks and lift the pallets, and the steering is in the back wheels, so it turns really sharp. I don't think they even have manual controls anymore, do they? Unless you're like a firefighter with a special key. So I'm not really sure if it would help. She has this massive collection of them under her desk. She was complaining about her feet hurting and wanted to take the elevator down from the fourth floor, and I just told her I'd meet her in the lobby. I just took the stairs. \n\nI've gotten pretty fast at taking the stairs, actually. I try to skip every other step on the way down, it kind of feels like a workout. I used to run cross-country in high school, so I guess I still have some of that stamina. We had this coach, Coach Miller, who would make us run hills in the pouring rain. He used to say it built character, but I think he just liked watching us suffer. \n\nBut yeah, I don't know if having someone with me in the elevator would help. He used to bring his Nintendo Switch and just play Zelda under the desk the whole time. Greg didn't even go help him, he just sat there laughing. He eventually got fired because he fell asleep on a night shift and someone stole a bunch of laptops from the third floor. \n\nSo yeah, if someone like Greg is the one monitoring the elevator, I definitely don't think that would make me feel any better. I just... I don't know, it's just the elevator itself, you know? But it's still just a box hanging by a wire, you know? \n\nSpeaking of operating stuff, though, at my job—I do training and development—we just had to roll out this massive new training module for the forklift drivers at our main warehouse. I mean, as long as I don't have to take an elevator to get up there, right? I actually went hiking up in the mountains a couple of years ago with some friends. We drove out to this trail—my buddy drove his Jeep, which was cool, but man, the suspension on those things is so stiff, I felt every single rock on the dirt road. We ended up at this overlook that was crazy high up, just a sheer drop-off. And I felt totally fine standing near the edge. \n\nWe actually brought a picnic up there. Sandwiches from this little deli near my place. They make this incredible spicy Italian sub, like, they use this special pepper relish that just makes the whole thing. I've tried to recreate it at home, but I can never get the vinegar ratio right. I think they might use some sort of artisan balsamic or something. But yeah, standing up there, looking out over the whole valley while eating that sandwich... it was great. No panic at all. So, no, it's definitely not a height thing.\n\nDoctor: What exactly do you think might happen if you were to get trapped in an elevator?\n\nPatient: I don't know, honestly. I guess I just picture the doors getting stuck and me just... being stuck in there forever. Or until the air runs out. Which I know doesn't actually happen, they aren't airtight. I saw this documentary once about how buildings are ventilated, and it's actually super fascinating. They have all these massive ducts and fans up on the roof, and the system is designed to keep the air pressure balanced throughout the whole building. \n\nThe guy in the documentary was explaining how they have to clean those ducts, and it looked like the worst job ever. They send these little remote-controlled robots with cameras and brushes on them down into the vents. I actually looked up how much those robots cost because I thought it would be a cool toy to mess around with, maybe attach a camera to it and see what my cat does when it chases him around the apartment. My cat, Barnaby, he's a trip. He's this orange tabby, and he has this weird obsession with knocking my pens off the desk. Every single time I sit down to work, swat, swat, there goes the pen. I had to buy a special heavy-duty pen holder just to keep him out of it. \n\nBut, um... yeah, getting trapped. I just... I don't really know what would happen, but the thought of it just makes my chest tight.\n\nDoctor: Is it the thought of being in a small, enclosed space like an elevator that scares you, or is it something more specific about elevators themselves?\n\nPatient: I think it's just elevators specifically. Like, I know an elevator in a nice, modern office block is probably completely safe, right? But when I look at those old, clunky doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at my work, my mind just immediately goes to this place where I'm convinced I'm about to get trapped in there, or the cables are going to snap and drop me. I work as a training specialist for this corporate tech company, and our building is from, like, the 1970s. The carpet in the hallways is this hideous orange and brown geometric pattern. It honestly looks like something out of a bad sci-fi movie. I was actually talking to the facilities manager about it last week—nice guy, his name is Dave, always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts. He was telling me that they're finally going to renovate the whole floor next spring. They're going to put in hardwood, or well, that fake laminate stuff that looks like hardwood, which is probably easier to clean anyway. I spilled coffee on that orange carpet on my second day of work, and let me tell you, getting a stain out of 40-year-old carpet is impossible. I tried club soda, dish soap, everything. I ended up just having to put a potted plant over the spot so my boss wouldn't see it. It's a snake plant, actually, because I read they're impossible to kill, and I have a terrible track record with plants. \n\nBut yeah... what was I saying? Oh, right. The old doors. Yeah, looking at those old elevator doors just makes my brain think I'm going to get stuck or dropped, even if I know it's probably fine.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is because you feel like you're not in control when you're inside one?\n\nPatient: I mean, maybe? I haven't really thought about it like that. Control is a weird thing, you know? I spent like twenty bucks just playing the Addams Family pinball machine. The flippers on it were perfectly calibrated, it was awesome. I had zero control over the situation, just sitting there in the passenger seat listening to him complain about the brake lights in front of us. \n\nHe was listening to this podcast about deep-sea diving, which honestly sounded terrifying. Just annoyed that we were going to be late for the arcade. So... yeah, I don't really know if it's a control thing with the elevators. I just really, really don't want to get in them.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would feel less anxious about elevators if you were in control of the elevator, for example, if you were the one operating it?\n\nPatient: I don't know, maybe? If I had like a joystick or something and I could steer it? But elevators don't really work like that, do they? You just push a button and hope for the best. It's not like driving a forklift. \n\nActually, I had to get certified to drive a forklift at my first job out of high school. It was this massive warehouse that distributed pet supplies. Dog food, cat litter, those giant scratching posts... you wouldn't believe how heavy a pallet of clumping cat litter is. I had to take this two-day training course, and the instructor was this old guy named Earl who chewed on unlit cigars the entire time. Never lit them, just chewed on them. He was super strict about the speed limit in the warehouse, which was like five miles an hour. It felt like you were crawling. You use these levers to tilt the forks and lift the pallets, and the steering is in the back wheels, so it turns really sharp. He used to say it built character, but I think he just liked watching us suffer. \n\nBut yeah, I don't know if having someone with me in the elevator would help. It's really just the elevators that freak me out. I don't know why.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators would decrease if you knew someone was constantly monitoring the elevator's systems and could intervene if something went wrong?\n\nPatient: I don't really know if that would help, honestly. Is it just some guy in a basement somewhere? \n\nBecause my buddy Greg used to work security for this big office building downtown, and his whole job was basically just watching camera feeds. I kept dropping stitches, and the thing I made ended up looking like a lopsided sock for a giant. She still has it in a box somewhere in her attic. Her attic is terrifying, by the way. I had to go up there last Thanksgiving to get the good gravy boat, and I swear one of them moved. \n\nBut wait, what did you ask me? A pattern of anxiety? Yeah, no, I don't think it's a whole pattern thing. It's just the elevators. I just don't like being stuck in them.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is connected to a more general anxiety about being in situations where things are out of your control?\n\nPatient: I mean, I don't really think it's some big, connected thing.
